problems.memo_sentence: "The paper claims that classical computing solutions to this type of crash-estimation problem would be computationally infeasible, citing an estimate of 13.7 billion years of runtime for classical methods on similar problems."
problems.source_evidence: "According to the work of Orus, Mugel and Lizaso [3], they stated that even with small networks (20-30 institutions), solving these type of problem takes 13.7 billion years with classical methods"
problems.explanation: The 13.7 billion-year estimate is explicitly attributed to prior work by Orus, Mugel, and Lizaso, not presented as a new result of this paper. The memo incorrectly frames it as the paper's own claim.

problems.memo_sentence: "The authors acknowledge several limitations: inadequate and incomplete financial information and inter-firm relations in the available data constrain the quality and feasibility of the constructed networks and require post-processing of equilibrium points."
problems.source_evidence: "Since current financial information and relations between the companies are inadequate equilibrium points required to be post-processed."
problems.explanation: The memo captures the post-processing issue, but it omits the paper's explicit limitation that the available financial information and inter-company relations are inadequate. That limitation is central to why post-processing is needed.

problems.memo_sentence: "On 2019 financial data, the model identifies 90.04 million TL of non-performing loans out of 107 million TL and reports an overall prediction accuracy of about 91.2%, with quarterly accuracy figures also reported."
problems.source_evidence: Abstract: "Using financial data from 2019, our model successfully identified 90.04 million TL out of 107 million TL of non-performing loans. Similarly, using data from 2020, it identified 669.92 million TL out of 726 million TL of non-performing loans. Overall, the model accurately predicted 91.2."
problems.explanation: The memo mentions the 2019 result and overall accuracy but omits the adjacent 2020 result in the same abstract passage. This is a selective summary of the reported results.

problems.memo_sentence: "The paper claims that classical computing solutions to this type of crash-estimation problem would be computationally infeasible, citing an estimate of 13.7 billion years of runtime for classical methods on similar problems. In contrast, the hybrid quantum approach reportedly solves the formulated optimization problem in seconds, though the extreme classical runtime figure is drawn from prior literature rather than measured directly in this study."
problems.source_evidence: "According to the work of Orus, Mugel and Lizaso [3], they stated that even with small networks (20-30 institutions), solving these type of problem takes 13.7 billion years with classical methods, yet with the mentioned Quantum Processing power we were able to solve the problem in a reasonable amount of time as 7 seconds per solution."
problems.explanation: The memo correctly notes the prior-literature origin of the classical runtime estimate, but it omits the paper's specific condition that the estimate applies to small networks of 20–30 institutions. That qualifier matters to the scope of the claim.

problems.memo_sentence: "The hybrid solver exhibits sensitivity to solve time: shorter-than-recommended times yield infeasible solutions with constraint violations, while longer runtimes do not improve results beyond obtaining feasible solutions."
problems.source_evidence: "When we wanted to solve the problem in a smaller amount of time the results we were getting were not feasible, meaning that there were constraint violations in the found solution. We have also tried raising the solution time but we have observed that going above the recommended solve time didn’t affect the results that we were getting are all feasible solutions."
problems.explanation: The memo captures the main sensitivity finding, but it softens the paper's stronger statement that longer runtimes did not affect the results at all beyond feasibility. The source presents this as an observed lack of improvement, not just a general tendency.
